questions.title: Relativity as an experimentally tested theory
questions.prompt: Give two examples discussed in this chapter in which special-relativistic effects can be tested or measured. For each, state the effect involved and explain what differs from the corresponding classical prediction. You may use research examples rather than everyday experiences.
questions.answer_check: Suitable examples include increased laboratory mean lifetimes of moving unstable particles, atmospheric muon survival explained consistently by time dilation and length contraction, and deviations of high-speed particle momentum/energy from classical predictions. Two descriptions of the same muon observation should not count as independent examples. If GPS is used, distinguish the special-relativistic contribution from gravitational effects.
questions.rationale: Restore the essay’s evidence-based synthesis; do not present cosmological redshift as purely a special-relativistic Doppler measurement.

questions.title: Explain what changed in your understanding
questions.prompt: In no more than 200 words, summarize the two postulates of special relativity and explain two consequences you learned in this chapter. Identify one everyday intuition that needs to change, and explain how classical predictions remain useful at low speeds.
questions.answer_check: Open response: accurate postulates including vacuum light speed; two correctly explained consequences; a specific misconception addressed; classical limit. No single prescribed example or wording.
questions.rationale: Retain the course’s broad reflection prompt as a review candidate; it can be removed later if it overlaps assigned essays.
